analysis.one_liner: Phases out the lower minimum wage for tipped workers so they earn the full federal minimum.
analysis.headline: The bill to phase out the $2.13 tipped minimum wage drew 25 cosponsors but never got a committee hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the separate, much lower minimum wage for tipped employees under federal law. During a multi-year phase-in, employers would pay tipped workers a rising cash wage starting at $3.60 an hour until it reaches the full federal minimum, ending the 'tip credit' that lets restaurants count tips toward the wage they owe. It also strengthens rules that workers keep their own tips, bars employers from skimming card-processing fees out of tips, creates a process for workers to vote on tip pools, and requires disclosure of what portion of mandatory service charges goes to employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Tipped workers — servers, bussers, and other employees who currently can be paid as little as $2.13 an hour in cash by their employer — would get a guaranteed rising cash wage regardless of tips, ending the risk that tips don't cover what an employer should have paid. Workers would also gain from stronger tip-retention rules and a say over tip pools.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the tip credit so the wage an employer must pay a tipped employee is the full federal minimum wage, not a lower tipped rate, with repeal taking effect once the transition wage reaches the standard minimum [S3].
Raises the cash wage during the phase-in to $3.60 an hour in the first year, then $1.50 more each following year, capped at the federal minimum [S3].

Rewrites the tipped-employee definition to add a rule that a worker is not 'tipped' for any workweek in which more than 20 percent of hours are nontipped duties, limiting misuse of the lower rate during the transition [S3].
Bars employers and managers from keeping any tips, and specifically bars using tips to cover credit and debit card transaction fees [S3].

Creates a vote process: if 30 percent of a business's non-supervisory employees request a vote on a tip pool, it is established if 51 percent vote yes; participation must be voluntary and the employer must administer it at its own expense [S3].
Requires disclosure of mandatory service charges, including the portion that will go to employees, and treats that portion as tips for tax purposes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Restaurant and other tipped-service employers, who would pay a rising cash wage instead of the $2.13 tipped minimum plus tip credit; costs could show up in higher menu prices or service charges, and card-processing fees could no longer be passed out of workers' tips.

drawbacks.text: The transition keeps a subminimum wage in place for several years: $3.60 the first year, then $1.50 annual increases, so tipped workers stay below the full minimum during the phase-in [S3].

The restaurant industry has long argued that eliminating the tip credit raises labor costs sharply for full-service restaurants and could mean reduced hours, fewer staff, or higher prices for customers; the bill gives employers no offsetting tax relief for the added wage cost.

Some servers at high-volume, high-tip restaurants who currently earn far above the minimum through tips could see changes to scheduling or tip-pooling practices as employers adjust to paying the full cash wage; the bill's tip-pool vote process leaves the employer administering the pool.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For tipped workers, the core benefit is large and concrete: a guaranteed cash wage that rises to the full federal minimum, so tips become income on top of a real wage rather than a subsidy to the employer's payroll. The costs fall on restaurant operators, who would face meaningfully higher payroll, and ultimately on customers through prices — a real but modest pass-through, since seven states already require the full minimum for tipped workers with no documented collapse of their restaurant sectors. The bill's design is reasonable but not aggressive: the multi-year phase-in and the retention of a subminimum during transition delay full protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two committees, and neither committee took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, so it simply expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Jahana Hayes introduced the Tipped Worker Protection Act in the House on July 19, 2022 [S1].
It was referred to the Committee on Education and Labor and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction [S5].
Twenty-five House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all in the same party as the sponsor [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the referrals — no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Restaurant and other tipped-service employers came out ahead: they continue to pay the $2.13 federal tipped minimum and count tips against wages owed, while the tipped workers the bill aimed to help gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and the record shows no Republican support; the bill was referred to committees controlled by the Democratic majority, which took no action.

industries.note: Restaurants would have to pay servers the full minimum wage in cash instead of $2.13 plus a tip credit, raising payroll significantly, and could no longer recoup card-processing fees out of tips. The industry's interest in the bill's defeat ran against the wage security of the workers it employs.

industries.industry: Other tipped-service employers (salons, car washes, casinos, delivery)
industries.note: Any employer using the tip credit would face the same rising cash wage requirement and the new tip-retention and service-charge disclosure rules.
The bill bars employers from using tips to cover card transaction fees, so processors could no longer be effectively paid out of workers' tips; merchants would absorb the fees instead.
